parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification of an alternating voltage.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what is different between an alternating supply that keeps changing direction and a direct supply that flows one way only - what change must rectification make?
parts.proper_answer: Rectification is the conversion of an alternating voltage or current into a direct (unidirectional) voltage or current.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture a.c. versus d.c.**
Think of a.c. as pushing then pulling, with voltage swinging positive then negative. Think of d.c. as pushing in one direction only. Rectification is the process that turns that two-way variation into a one-way output.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State the difference between half-wave rectification and full-wave rectification.

markscheme_points.text: half-wave: voltage in one direction is removed
full-wave: voltage in one direction is reversed

hints: Hint 1: Focus on what happens to the half of the a.c. cycle that is in the unwanted direction - is it simply lost or is it kept in some way?
Hint 2: Compare blocking one polarity completely with flipping one polarity over so both halves end up on the same side.
parts.proper_answer: In half-wave rectification the voltage of one polarity is removed (blocked), so output exists for only half of each cycle. In full-wave rectification the voltage of one polarity is reversed, so both halves of each cycle appear as output in the same direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Half-wave means half is missing**
With a single diode, current can pass one way but not the other. So for one half-cycle you get an output, for the next half-cycle you get zero. One direction is removed.

Step 2: **Full-wave means nothing is wasted**
With a bridge of diodes, the negative half-cycle is not blocked, it is turned upside down. Both positive and negative input halves give a positive output, so you get twice as many pulses.

parts.label: (b)(i)

markscheme_points.text: one gap connected by a single diode and other gap connected directly
diode drawn (in a circuit) with correct circuit symbol

hints: Hint 1: For half-wave you need current to reach the resistor on only one half-cycle - where must a one-way device go to control the whole output?
Hint 2: Remember one input lead can go straight through to the output side, but the other lead needs the diode in series, drawn as a triangle pointing toward a bar.
parts.proper_answer: Connect one $V_{IN}$ lead directly to the lower common line of C and R. Connect the other $V_{IN}$ lead to the upper common line of C and R through a single diode in series, using the correct diode symbol.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Place the diode in series**
You have two gaps between $V_{IN}$ on the left and the C-R parallel combination on the right. Leave the bottom gap as a plain wire. Put a single diode in the top gap so all current to the resistor must go through it.

Step 2: **Use the correct symbol**
Draw the diode as a triangle with its point touching a short bar: $\triangleright |$. Either orientation gives half-wave action, it just selects which half-cycle is passed. This allows conduction in one direction only and blocks the opposite half-cycle.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: Show that the capacitance of C is $570\ \mu\text{F}$.
hints: Hint 1: Start from Fig. 6.3 and identify the maximum value of $V_{OUT}$ - this is the voltage across C when it stores maximum energy.
Hint 2: Link stored energy to capacitance and that peak voltage, then rearrange to find $C$ and convert to $\mu\text{F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the peak voltage**
From Fig. 6.3 the maximum $V_{OUT}$ is $12\text{ V}$. This is the voltage across the parallel capacitor at maximum charge, so use $V = 12\text{ V}$ and $E = 0.041\text{ J}$.

Step 2: **Rearrange and calculate**
Energy in a capacitor is $$E = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$$ so $$C = \frac{2E}{V^2}$$ Substituting: $$C = \frac{2 \times 0.041}{12^2} = \frac{0.082}{144} \approx 5.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$$ Since $1\,\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\text{ F}$, this is about $570\,\mu\text{F}$, as required.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 6.3 for a discharge section where $V_{OUT}$ falls smoothly - what are the start voltage, end voltage and time taken for that fall?
Hint 2: Recall how voltage decays with time when a capacitor discharges through a resistor, and think about which time interval corresponds to $t$ in that relation.
Hint 3: Take natural logs to isolate $R$, using your value of $C \approx 5.7 \times 10^{-4}\text{ F}$ from (c)(i).
parts.proper_answer: $V = V_0 \exp(-t/RC)$ with $V_0 = 12.0\text{ V}$ falling to $8.0\text{ V}$ in $t = 0.010\text{ s}$ gives $R \approx 43\,\Omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the discharge**
From $t = 0.01\text{ s}$ to $t = 0.02\text{ s}$ in Fig. 6.3, $V_{IN}$ is negative so the diode blocks and C discharges through R. Voltage falls from $V_0 = 12\text{ V}$ to $V = 8.0\text{ V}$ in time $t = 0.010\text{ s}$.

Step 2: **Apply exponential discharge**
For discharge: $$V = V_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t}{RC}\right)$$ So: $$8.0 = 12.0 \exp\left(-\frac{0.010}{RC}\right)$$

Step 3: **Solve for R**
Take natural logs: $$\ln\left(\frac{8.0}{12.0}\right) = -\frac{0.010}{R \times 5.7 \times 10^{-4}}$$ $$-0.405 = -\frac{0.010}{R \times 5.7 \times 10^{-4}}$$ $$R = \frac{0.010}{0.405 \times 5.7 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 43\,\Omega$$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at where C is connected - directly across R - and think about what a capacitor does when the rectified voltage tries to fall to zero.
parts.proper_answer: Smoothing - to store charge when $V_{OUT}$ is high and release it when $V_{OUT}$ would otherwise fall, reducing variation (ripple) in $V_{OUT}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Capacitor as a reservoir**
The capacitor charges up to the peak rectified voltage. When the diode stops conducting and the supply would drop to zero, the capacitor discharges through R, keeping $V_{OUT}$ high. That smooths the pulses into a steadier d.c. voltage.
